Confirming one of Apple 's worst-kept secrets, Apple finally unveiled its first-ever touchscreen MacBook Pro in 14-inch and 16-inch models on Wednesday, October 28, in Los Angeles. The news comes just days after Apple unveiled M6-class MacBook Pros . Notably, the new PROLED touchscreen laptops are running M5 Pro and M5 Max Apple silicon. Apple CEO John Ternus didn't waste much time on stage, quickly announcing the laptops and running through key innovations like the tandem OLED (PROLED) screens and relatively lightweight (3lbs for the 14-inch model and 4lbs for the 16-inch one) before leaving the stage and directing the assembled group of media, analysts, creators, and Apple execs to an adjacent space where I got my first experience ever with a touchscreen MacBook. If you read no further, know this: it felt totally natural to tap, swipe, gesture with three fingers, pinch, zoom, and more on a MacBook Pro display. It feels like I've been waiting my whole life to do this on a MacBook (or at least as long as I've been using MacBooks). As a former Windows user, and more specifically a longtime Surface Pro fan, I'm actually quite used to touching a screen, though maybe not one quite as beautiful as this. For those unfamiliar with tandem OLED technology, which Apple first introduced a few years ago with the iPad Pro, it sandwiches two ultra-thin, light-emitting OLEDs together. This increases the brightness while maintaining incredibly inky blacks (they're gorgeous). It also allows for a far thinner display panel because you don't need a backlight. Though there now is a "backlight of a sort. This touchscreen MacBook Pro lineup marks the return of the glowing Apple logo on the back of the display. It lights up when you open the laptop and turns off when you close it (people at the Hollywood, California, event were cheering for that). I played mostly with the larger, 16-inch model, which still features the expansive, backlit Magic Keyboard and a huge ForceTouch Trackpad, which honestly is gonna get a little bit less use now that a touchscreen is just inches away. A pair of large speaker grills sits on either side of the keyboard, though I couldn't hear them over the din of the demo room. As with previous MacBook Pros, there's still an SD Card slot, three Thunderbolt 5 ports, one USB-4 port, HDMI, and the headphone jack. In my hands, the 4 lb, 16-inch model felt a tad lighter than previous 16-inch MacBook Pros, though the 14-inch (which might be my preference) felt lightweight at 3lbs. Let's talk, though, about using the touchscreen. I tried a 3D design app where I used a couple of fingers to spin a model of a guy in battle armor and then a single finger to paint gold on some of the armor. I opened Maps and used two fingers to spin the map, then pinch-and-zoom. I used three fingers to swipe through desktops. I could use two fingers to grab a window, flip it to one side of the screen, and watch it instantly dock itself as a half-screen app (yes, I've done something very similar on a Surface Pro). I played touchscreen piano with all my fingers. At no moment did I hesitate and wonder how I did this or that thing. It's obvious. It never felt uncomfortable, and my arm never got tired. Put another way, a touchscreen is a perfect fit for the MacBook Pro family, Now, you cannot take the screen and flip it all the way to the back of the laptop (something many touchscreen Windows laptops can do). That might be a shame because I could also use my finger to paint and, though I haven't done it yet, draw. Speaking of which, there is no indication that the touchscreen MacBook Pro supports the Apple Pencil. Honestly, if it can't fold back at least flat, there's no point in this support anyway. There is, by the way, a Dynamic Island that's basically copied from the iPhone, but I didn't see it do very much. As I used the touchscreen MacBook Pro, I was not only reminded of my time with the Microsoft Surface Pro but of my initial weeks and even months with the MacBook after I switched platforms. Yes, I found myself touching the inert MacBook screen and had to retrain myself to stop doing it. Point is, touch was something I reflexively used on the Surface Pro, and I am now certain I will happily use it on the touchscreen MacBook Pro. You probably will, too. You will pay for the privilege of touch. The 14-inch MacBook Pro with touch starts at $2,899 / £2,899 / AU$4,599, and the 16-inch model starts at $3,399 / £3,399 / $5,499. Confirming one of Apple 's worst-kept secrets, Apple finally unveiled its first-ever touchscreen MacBook Pro in 14-inch and 16-inch models on Wednesday, October 28, in Los Angeles. The news comes just days after Apple unveiled M6-class MacBook Pros . Notably, the new PROLED touchscreen laptops are running M5 Pro and M5 Max Apple silicon.

Apple CEO John Ternus didn't waste much time on stage, quickly announcing the laptops and running through key innovations like the tandem OLED (PROLED) screens and relatively lightweight (3lbs for the 14-inch model and 4lbs for the 16-inch one) before leaving the stage and directing the assembled group of media, analysts, creators, and Apple execs to an adjacent space where I got my first experience ever with a touchscreen MacBook.

If you read no further, know this: it felt totally natural to tap, swipe, gesture with three fingers, pinch, zoom, and more on a MacBook Pro display. It feels like I've been waiting my whole life to do this on a MacBook (or at least as long as I've been using MacBooks).
As a former Windows user, and more specifically a longtime Surface Pro fan, I'm actually quite used to touching a screen, though maybe not one quite as beautiful as this.

For those unfamiliar with tandem OLED technology, which Apple first introduced a few years ago with the iPad Pro, it sandwiches two ultra-thin, light-emitting OLEDs together. This increases the brightness while maintaining incredibly inky blacks (they're gorgeous). It also allows for a far thinner display panel because you don't need a backlight.

Though there now is a "backlight of a sort. This touchscreen MacBook Pro lineup marks the return of the glowing Apple logo on the back of the display. It lights up when you open the laptop and turns off when you close it (people at the Hollywood, California, event were cheering for that).

I played mostly with the larger, 16-inch model, which still features the expansive, backlit Magic Keyboard and a huge ForceTouch Trackpad, which honestly is gonna get a little bit less use now that a touchscreen is just inches away.

A pair of large speaker grills sits on either side of the keyboard, though I couldn't hear them over the din of the demo room. As with previous MacBook Pros, there's still an SD Card slot, three Thunderbolt 5 ports, one USB-4 port, HDMI, and the headphone jack.
In my hands, the 4 lb, 16-inch model felt a tad lighter than previous 16-inch MacBook Pros, though the 14-inch (which might be my preference) felt lightweight at 3lbs.
Let's talk, though, about using the touchscreen.
I tried a 3D design app where I used a couple of fingers to spin a model of a guy in battle armor and then a single finger to paint gold on some of the armor.
I opened Maps and used two fingers to spin the map, then pinch-and-zoom.
I used three fingers to swipe through desktops.
I could use two fingers to grab a window, flip it to one side of the screen, and watch it instantly dock itself as a half-screen app (yes, I've done something very similar on a Surface Pro).
I played touchscreen piano with all my fingers.

At no moment did I hesitate and wonder how I did this or that thing. It's obvious. It never felt uncomfortable, and my arm never got tired. Put another way, a touchscreen is a perfect fit for the MacBook Pro family,

Now, you cannot take the screen and flip it all the way to the back of the laptop (something many touchscreen Windows laptops can do). That might be a shame because I could also use my finger to paint and, though I haven't done it yet, draw.
Speaking of which, there is no indication that the touchscreen MacBook Pro supports the Apple Pencil. Honestly, if it can't fold back at least flat, there's no point in this support anyway.
There is, by the way, a Dynamic Island that's basically copied from the iPhone, but I didn't see it do very much.

As I used the touchscreen MacBook Pro, I was not only reminded of my time with the Microsoft Surface Pro but of my initial weeks and even months with the MacBook after I switched platforms. Yes, I found myself touching the inert MacBook screen and had to retrain myself to stop doing it.
Point is, touch was something I reflexively used on the Surface Pro, and I am now certain I will happily use it on the touchscreen MacBook Pro. You probably will, too.

You will pay for the privilege of touch. The 14-inch MacBook Pro with touch starts at $2,899 / £2,899 / AU$4,599, and the 16-inch model starts at $3,399 / £3,399 / $5,499. Pre-orders are live today, and the laptops ship on November 6.

Both sizes use Apple’s M5 Pro or M5 Max chips, and both go on sale November 6, 2026. For a company that spent more than a decade steering Mac owners toward the keyboard and trackpad, this is a real reversal. We tracked the build-up in our earlier look at the Pro and tell launch expectations , and the final product matches the broad outline. This analysis covers what Apple confirmed, what it left open, how the pricing compares with the rest of the market, and what the touchscreen MacBook Pro means for buyers, developers and rival laptop makers. Apple calls the product the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display, and coverage identifies it as the company’s first laptop with a touch-sensitive screen. It ships in two sizes, 14 inches and 16 inches. Apple’s M5 Pro and M5 Max chips power the lineup. The company showed the machines at its “Pro and tell” event, where John Ternus, identified in coverage as Apple’s CEO, unveiled the touchscreen MacBooks. The headline feature is simple to state. You can now touch the Mac’s screen and expect it to respond. The harder question is what that changes in daily use. Apple has not turned the MacBook Pro into a tablet. The hardware stays a clamshell laptop with a keyboard and trackpad, and the touch layer sits on top of the existing Mac experience. How deeply macOS adapts to fingers, and which apps get touch-native controls on day one, remain open points that the announcement coverage does not settle. The Verge published the reveal video for the touchscreen MacBook Pro , which gives the clearest first look at how Apple chose to present the change. CNN Business framed the news more bluntly, with a headline that called it Apple’s first-ever MacBook with a touchscreen. Reuters, Ars Technica and other outlets reached the same conclusion. The story is not that Apple copied a Windows feature. The story is that Apple moved at all. Three facts anchor everything else in this piece. First, the display technology is new to the MacBook Pro line. Second, the price floor sits well above where most people expect a laptop to start. Third, the on-sale date is only nine days away, so Apple has little time to let rumor fill the gaps. Those three facts shape the rest of the analysis below. The 14-inch touchscreen MacBook Pro starts at $2,899. The 16-inch starts at $3,399. The gap between the two sizes is exactly $500, or roughly 17% on top of the smaller model’s base price. Apple has not published a wider configuration list in the material we verified, so those two numbers are the only prices we can state with confidence. BNN Bloomberg’s report on the first touchscreen laptops arriving amid a product blitz placed the launch inside a busy stretch for Apple, and that context matters for pricing. When a company launches several products in a short window, it usually prices the newest halo item high and lets cheaper models absorb the volume. A $2,899 entry point reads as a halo price, aimed at buyers who already pay for top-end Pro hardware. Pricing tells you who Apple expects to buy first. At these levels the customer is a working professional, a studio, or a company that buys machines in batches and writes them off. Casual users who want a touchscreen laptop for browsing and video calls have cheaper options on the Windows side. Apple appears comfortable ceding that segment for now. The panel is where the money goes. Apple’s reported specifications describe a tandem OLED display with up to 2,000 nits of brightness, a 10,000,000:1 contrast ratio and a refresh rate of up to 120Hz. Tandem OLED stacks two emissive layers, which generally lets a panel reach higher brightness and last longer than a single-layer design. Apple has not, in the verified material, published lifetime or burn-in data for the new panel, so treat durability as an open question. Pairing a touch layer with OLED also creates engineering tradeoffs that Apple has not discussed in the verified coverage. Touch sensors, a protective surface and a glare-control finish all affect how a screen looks under bright light. Reviewers will test those tradeoffs once units reach them. Until then, the spec sheet tells you the ceiling and the review bench will tell you the reality. Apple chose its M5 Pro and M5 Max chips for the new machines. We have no verified CPU or GPU core counts, memory ceilings, storage ceilings or battery-life numbers, so this section sticks to what is solid. The pairing signals that Apple sees the touchscreen MacBook Pro as a premium creative and engineering tool rather than a general-purpose entry laptop. Chip choice also frames the competition. Our own Apple Silicon vs Intel MacBook Pro comparison looked at how the M5 Max stacks up against Intel’s top mobile part, and the memory bandwidth gap was a central point. Apple’s advantage in efficiency per watt has shaped laptop buying for several years. Adding a touchscreen does not change that equation, but it does raise the question of what the new panel costs in battery life, a number Apple has not confirmed. The wider architecture story is covered in our ARM vs x86 analysis . The short version is that Apple’s unified memory design and its controlled software stack let it tune hardware and macOS together. coreStoryFacts.text: The MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display — man, that's a lot of words for a laptop — comes a day after Apple debuted upgraded versions of its MacBook Pro and iMac .
The company kicked off the week with a refresh to its iPad mini , which received a larger, improved display and a new processor.
The base MacBook Pro 14-inch with Apple's new M6 processor starts at $1,999.
It's also where you'll find Siri AI and Live Activities.
Apple's move to include a touchscreen display with its MacBook comes years after rivals Microsoft ( MSFT ), HP ( HPQ ), Dell ( DELL ), and others implemented the technology in their own laptops.
Yahoo Finance is not a broker-dealer or investment adviser and does not offer securities or cryptocurrencies for sale or facilitate trading.
Apple's Mac line of devices accounted for $33.7 billion of the company's $416.1 billion in 2025, making it the tech giant's fourth-largest segment by sales.
Those prices represent a $300 increase that Apple implemented in June due to the global memory and storage shortage.
Apple previously dabbled with touch on its Macs with its Touch Bar, a thin touch-sensitive OLED strip that sat above the keyboard.
But the company discarded the feature after it failed to gain traction among users.
Inside, the notebooks can be outfitted with either Apple's M5 Pro or M5 Max processors.
Confirming one of Apple 's worst-kept secrets, Apple finally unveiled its first-ever touchscreen MacBook Pro in 14-inch and 16-inch models on Wednesday, October 28, in Los Angeles.
The news comes just days after Apple unveiled M6-class MacBook Pros .
Notably, the new PROLED touchscreen laptops are running M5 Pro and M5 Max Apple silicon.
Yes, I found myself touching the inert MacBook screen and had to retrain myself to stop doing it.
If you read no further, know this: it felt totally natural to tap, swipe, gesture with three fingers, pinch, zoom, and more on a MacBook Pro display.
It lights up when you open the laptop and turns off when you close it (people at the Hollywood, California, event were cheering for that).
Honestly, if it can't fold back at least flat, there's no point in this support anyway.
Pre-orders are live today, and the laptops ship on November 6.
At no moment did I hesitate and wonder how I did this or that thing.
It never felt uncomfortable, and my arm never got tired.
Put another way, a touchscreen is a perfect fit for the MacBook Pro family,
As a former Windows user, and more specifically a longtime Surface Pro fan, I'm actually quite used to touching a screen, though maybe not one quite as beautiful as this.
For those unfamiliar with tandem OLED technology, which Apple first introduced a few years ago with the iPad Pro, it sandwiches two ultra-thin, light-emitting OLEDs together.

sources.title: I tried Apple's new touchscreen MacBook Pro, and touching a MacBook screen feels wonderfully natural - TechRadar
passages: Confirming one of Apple 's worst-kept secrets, Apple finally unveiled its first-ever touchscreen MacBook Pro in 14-inch and 16-inch models on Wednesday, October 28, in Los Angeles.
The news comes just days after Apple unveiled M6-class MacBook Pros .
Notably, the new PROLED touchscreen laptops are running M5 Pro and M5 Max Apple silicon.
Yes, I found myself touching the inert MacBook screen and had to retrain myself to stop doing it.
If you read no further, know this: it felt totally natural to tap, swipe, gesture with three fingers, pinch, zoom, and more on a MacBook Pro display.
It lights up when you open the laptop and turns off when you close it (people at the Hollywood, California, event were cheering for that).
Honestly, if it can't fold back at least flat, there's no point in this support anyway.
Pre-orders are live today, and the laptops ship on November 6.
At no moment did I hesitate and wonder how I did this or that thing.
It never felt uncomfortable, and my arm never got tired.
Put another way, a touchscreen is a perfect fit for the MacBook Pro family,
As a former Windows user, and more specifically a longtime Surface Pro fan, I'm actually quite used to touching a screen, though maybe not one quite as beautiful as this.
For those unfamiliar with tandem OLED technology, which Apple first introduced a few years ago with the iPad Pro, it sandwiches two ultra-thin, light-emitting OLEDs together.
This increases the brightness while maintaining incredibly inky blacks (they're gorgeous).
It also allows for a far thinner display panel because you don't need a backlight.

Confirming one of Apple 's worst-kept secrets, Apple finally unveiled its first-ever touchscreen MacBook Pro in 14-inch and 16-inch models on Wednesday, October 28, in Los Angeles. The news comes just days after Apple unveiled M6-class MacBook Pros . Notably, the new PROLED touchscreen laptops are running M5 Pro and M5 Max Apple silicon. Apple CEO John Ternus didn't waste much time on stage, quickly announcing the laptops and running through key innovations like the tandem OLED (PROLED) screens and relatively lightweight (3lbs for the 14-inch model and 4lbs for the 16-inch one) before leaving the stage and directing the assembled group of media, analysts, creators, and Apple execs to an adjacent space where I got my first experience ever with a touchscreen MacBook. If you read no further, know this: it felt totally natural to tap, swipe, gesture with three fingers, pinch, zoom, and more on a MacBook Pro display. It feels like I've been waiting my whole life to do this on a MacBook (or at least as long as I've been using MacBooks). As a former Windows user, and more specifically a longtime Surface Pro fan, I'm actually quite used to touching a screen, though maybe not one quite as beautiful as this. For those unfamiliar with tandem OLED technology, which Apple first introduced a few years ago with the iPad Pro, it sandwiches two ultra-thin, light-emitting OLEDs together. This increases the brightness while maintaining incredibly inky blacks (they're gorgeous). It also allows for a far thinner display panel because you don't need a backlight. Though there now is a "backlight of a sort. This touchscreen MacBook Pro lineup marks the return of the glowing Apple logo on the back of the display. It lights up when you open the laptop and turns off when you close it (people at the Hollywood, California, event were cheering for that). I played mostly with the larger, 16-inch model, which still features the expansive, backlit Magic Keyboard and a huge ForceTouch Trackpad, which honestly is gonna get a little bit less use now that a touchscreen is just inches away. A pair of large speaker grills sits on either side of the keyboard, though I couldn't hear them over the din of the demo room. As with previous MacBook Pros, there's still an SD Card slot, three Thunderbolt 5 ports, one USB-4 port, HDMI, and the headphone jack. In my hands, the 4 lb, 16-inch model felt a tad lighter than previous 16-inch MacBook Pros, though the 14-inch (which might be my preference) felt lightweight at 3lbs. Let's talk, though, about using the touchscreen. I tried a 3D design app where I used a couple of fingers to spin a model of a guy in battle armor and then a single finger to paint gold on some of the armor. I opened Maps and used two fingers to spin the map, then pinch-and-zoom. I used three fingers to swipe through desktops. I could use two fingers to grab a window, flip it to one side of the screen, and watch it instantly dock itself as a half-screen app (yes, I've done something very similar on a Surface Pro). I played touchscreen piano with all my fingers. At no moment did I hesitate and wonder how I did this or that thing. It's obvious. It never felt uncomfortable, and my arm never got tired. Put another way, a touchscreen is a perfect fit for the MacBook Pro family, Now, you cannot take the screen and flip it all the way to the back of the laptop (something many touchscreen Windows laptops can do). That might be a shame because I could also use my finger to paint and, though I haven't done it yet, draw. Speaking of which, there is no indication that the touchscreen MacBook Pro supports the Apple Pencil. Honestly, if it can't fold back at least flat, there's no point in this support anyway. There is, by the way, a Dynamic Island that's basically copied from the iPhone, but I didn't see it do very much. As I used the touchscreen MacBook Pro, I was not only reminded of my time with the Microsoft Surface Pro but of my initial weeks and even months with the MacBook after I switched platforms. Yes, I found myself touching the inert MacBook screen and had to retrain myself to stop doing it. Point is, touch was something I reflexively used on the Surface Pro, and I am now certain I will happily use it on the touchscreen MacBook Pro. You probably will, too. You will pay for the privilege of touch. The 14-inch MacBook Pro with touch starts at $2,899 / £2,899 / AU$4,599, and the 16-inch model starts at $3,399 / £3,399 / $5,499. The news comes just days after Apple unveiled M6-class MacBook Pros . Notably, the new PROLED touchscreen laptops are running M5 Pro and M5 Max Apple silicon.

Apple CEO John Ternus didn't waste much time on stage, quickly announcing the laptops and running through key innovations like the tandem OLED (PROLED) screens and relatively lightweight (3lbs for the 14-inch model and 4lbs for the 16-inch one) before leaving the stage and directing the assembled group of media, analysts, creators, and Apple execs to an adjacent space where I got my first experience ever with a touchscreen MacBook.

If you read no further, know this: it felt totally natural to tap, swipe, gesture with three fingers, pinch, zoom, and more on a MacBook Pro display. It feels like I've been waiting my whole life to do this on a MacBook (or at least as long as I've been using MacBooks).
As a former Windows user, and more specifically a longtime Surface Pro fan, I'm actually quite used to touching a screen, though maybe not one quite as beautiful as this.

For those unfamiliar with tandem OLED technology, which Apple first introduced a few years ago with the iPad Pro, it sandwiches two ultra-thin, light-emitting OLEDs together. This increases the brightness while maintaining incredibly inky blacks (they're gorgeous). It also allows for a far thinner display panel because you don't need a backlight.

Though there now is a "backlight of a sort. This touchscreen MacBook Pro lineup marks the return of the glowing Apple logo on the back of the display. It lights up when you open the laptop and turns off when you close it (people at the Hollywood, California, event were cheering for that).

I played mostly with the larger, 16-inch model, which still features the expansive, backlit Magic Keyboard and a huge ForceTouch Trackpad, which honestly is gonna get a little bit less use now that a touchscreen is just inches away.

A pair of large speaker grills sits on either side of the keyboard, though I couldn't hear them over the din of the demo room. As with previous MacBook Pros, there's still an SD Card slot, three Thunderbolt 5 ports, one USB-4 port, HDMI, and the headphone jack.
In my hands, the 4 lb, 16-inch model felt a tad lighter than previous 16-inch MacBook Pros, though the 14-inch (which might be my preference) felt lightweight at 3lbs.
Let's talk, though, about using the touchscreen.
I tried a 3D design app where I used a couple of fingers to spin a model of a guy in battle armor and then a single finger to paint gold on some of the armor.
I opened Maps and used two fingers to spin the map, then pinch-and-zoom.
I used three fingers to swipe through desktops.
I could use two fingers to grab a window, flip it to one side of the screen, and watch it instantly dock itself as a half-screen app (yes, I've done something very similar on a Surface Pro).
I played touchscreen piano with all my fingers.

At no moment did I hesitate and wonder how I did this or that thing. It's obvious. It never felt uncomfortable, and my arm never got tired. Put another way, a touchscreen is a perfect fit for the MacBook Pro family,

Now, you cannot take the screen and flip it all the way to the back of the laptop (something many touchscreen Windows laptops can do). That might be a shame because I could also use my finger to paint and, though I haven't done it yet, draw.
Speaking of which, there is no indication that the touchscreen MacBook Pro supports the Apple Pencil. Honestly, if it can't fold back at least flat, there's no point in this support anyway.
There is, by the way, a Dynamic Island that's basically copied from the iPhone, but I didn't see it do very much.

As I used the touchscreen MacBook Pro, I was not only reminded of my time with the Microsoft Surface Pro but of my initial weeks and even months with the MacBook after I switched platforms. Yes, I found myself touching the inert MacBook screen and had to retrain myself to stop doing it.
Point is, touch was something I reflexively used on the Surface Pro, and I am now certain I will happily use it on the touchscreen MacBook Pro. You probably will, too.

You will pay for the privilege of touch. The 14-inch MacBook Pro with touch starts at $2,899 / £2,899 / AU$4,599, and the 16-inch model starts at $3,399 / £3,399 / $5,499. Pre-orders are live today, and the laptops ship on November 6.

Apple calls the product the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display, and coverage identifies it as the company’s first laptop with a touch-sensitive screen. The company showed the machines at its “Pro and tell” event, where John Ternus, identified in coverage as Apple’s CEO, unveiled the touchscreen MacBooks.

The headline feature is simple to state. You can now touch the Mac’s screen and expect it to respond. The harder question is what that changes in daily use. Apple has not turned the MacBook Pro into a tablet. The hardware stays a clamshell laptop with a keyboard and trackpad, and the touch layer sits on top of the existing Mac experience. How deeply macOS adapts to fingers, and which apps get touch-native controls on day one, remain open points that the announcement coverage does not settle.

The Verge published the reveal video for the touchscreen MacBook Pro , which gives the clearest first look at how Apple chose to present the change. CNN Business framed the news more bluntly, with a headline that called it Apple’s first-ever MacBook with a touchscreen. Reuters, Ars Technica and other outlets reached the same conclusion. The story is not that Apple copied a Windows feature. The story is that Apple moved at all.

Three facts anchor everything else in this piece. First, the display technology is new to the MacBook Pro line. Second, the price floor sits well above where most people expect a laptop to start. Third, the on-sale date is only nine days away, so Apple has little time to let rumor fill the gaps. Those three facts shape the rest of the analysis below.

The 14-inch touchscreen MacBook Pro starts at $2,899. The 16-inch starts at $3,399. The gap between the two sizes is exactly $500, or roughly 17% on top of the smaller model’s base price. Apple has not published a wider configuration list in the material we verified, so those two numbers are the only prices we can state with confidence.

passages: Stablecoin issuer Tether said it had frozen nearly $1.57 billion in assets linked to the incident, while Circle froze more than $800 million.
It gave no update on the status of the remaining $3.3 billion as Binance co-founder Yi He said the company would cover "all ‌hacking losses".

Oct 29 (Reuters) - Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, said a security breach had resulted in an estimated $6.3 billion impact that analysts said could amount to the biggest crypto heist ever and might make investors rethink the risks of owning digital assets.
Binance's Yi said $27 million in stablecoins ‌and about $2 million worth of World Liberty tokens had been frozen.
"User funds remain safe," Binance said in a statement.

"As a precaution, all deposits and withdrawals are temporarily suspended while our security teams conduct checks, secure wallet infrastructure, and trace affected ​assets, ​with the close support of our law enforcement and industry partners."
Bitcoin dropped more than 3% to a six-week low of $76,368 and ether fell more than 3% to a two-month low of $2,178.
BNB, a token originally launched as Binance Coin that can be used to pay Binance fees, was down 5% over the past 24 hours at $709.70, according to market aggregator CoinGecko.
Binance runs a secure ​asset fund for users, which is a reserve held entirely in bitcoin that ‌is intended to protect user assets in cases of security breaches, according to its website.
Miguel Morel, CEO of blockchain intelligence firm Arkham, said data indicated that billions of dollars appeared to have been hacked from Binance ‌by an unknown actor.
The incident adds to a string of crypto thefts. ​Last year, attackers stole $2.9 billion worth of cryptocurrency across ​nearly 150 attacks, according to researchers at TRM Labs.

An initial investigation suggested the breach may have started with a hacked laptop belonging to one of its engineers, which let an attacker gain access to one of its systems and make unauthorized withdrawals, Binance said.

Beyond the potential loss of assets, the security breach was ⁠likely to have wider ramifications for crypto, which had already been under pressure lately due to higher US interest rates and softer demand from exchange-traded fund buyers, analysts said.
"It's the biggest hack in history," said Aravind Srinivasan, head of large crypto market maker GSR's systematic ‌OTC business.

extraction.body: The world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, Binance, has frozen around $3 billion worth of digital assets after reporting a potential security breach. The incident has also prompted two major cryptocurrency firms, Tether and Circle, to freeze another $2.4 billion in assets linked to the suspected attack. Binance has temporarily suspended all deposits and withdrawals as its security teams investigate the incident. The company has also assured users that it will cover all losses arising from the security issue. The scale of the potential breach remains unclear. Blockchain analytics firms have estimated that the incident could involve more than $5 billion in stolen cryptocurrency, although Binance has not confirmed how much, if any, has been stolen. The security incident concerns Binance.com, the company's main global trading platform. Its US-focused subsidiary, Binance.US, said it was not affected. The developments have unsettled cryptocurrency markets. Bitcoin fell to a six-week low of $77,646 on Friday, October 30, while Ether dropped to a two-month low of $2,238.76, according to CoinGecko data cited by Reuters. Binance's native token, BNB, also fell more than 8 per cent over 24 hours to around $694. Binance said its teams had frozen approximately $3 billion worth of digital assets as part of efforts to contain the security incident. The exchange is working with law enforcement agencies, cryptocurrency issuers, blockchain intelligence firms and other industry partners to trace and freeze additional assets. The amount could increase as the investigation progresses. Two major cryptocurrency companies have also taken action. Tether, the issuer of the USDT stablecoin, said it had frozen around $1.6 billion in assets connected to the potential Binance hack. Circle, which issues the USDC stablecoin, said it had frozen more than $800 million linked to the incident. Together, the two companies have frozen around $2.4 billion in assets. The potential scale of the incident remains a major concern for the cryptocurrency industry. Glassnode, a digital asset analytics and advisory firm, estimated that the incident could involve around $5.3 billion in cryptocurrency. New York-based blockchain analytics firm Chainalysis put the estimated amount at more than $5.9 billion. These figures have not been confirmed by Binance and should not be treated as verified losses. If the higher estimate is established, the incident would rank among the largest cryptocurrency thefts on record. That incident resulted in losses of around $1.5 billion and has been attributed to hackers linked to North Korea. Binance has not disclosed the precise nature of the vulnerability or explained how the suspected attackers may have gained access to the assets. The company's former chief executive Changpeng Zhao also weighed in on the incident. "It does look like a hack," Zhao said in a post on X. He no longer runs Binance but remains a major shareholder in the company. What has Binance said about the security breach? Binance initially said its teams were investigating reports of a potential security issue and assured customers that their funds were safe. The company subsequently announced that it had frozen around $3 billion in assets. As a precaution, it suspended deposits and withdrawals while its security teams conducted checks and worked with law enforcement agencies to trace the funds. Binance also promised to compensate users for any losses. Binance will cover all losses," the company said in an update on X. It added that it was working around the clock and would publish a detailed post-mortem report once the investigation was complete. Why have Bitcoin and other cryptocurrencies fallen?

Binance's Yi said $27 million in stablecoins ‌and about $2 million worth of World Liberty tokens had been frozen.

Oct 29 (Reuters) - Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, said a security breach had resulted in an estimated $6.3 billion impact that analysts said could amount to the biggest crypto heist ever and might make investors rethink the risks of owning digital assets. Binance said it had worked with partners to freeze the ‌affected assets, with about $3 billion located so far. It gave no update on the status of the remaining $3.3 billion as Binance co-founder Yi He said the company would cover "all ‌hacking losses". An initial investigation suggested the breach may have started with a hacked laptop belonging to one of its engineers, which let an attacker gain access to one of its systems and make unauthorized withdrawals, Binance said. Markets reacted immediately in early ​Asian trading on Friday. Bitcoin dropped more than 3% to a six-week low of $76,368 and ether fell more than 3% to a two-month low of $2,178. BNB, a token originally launched as Binance Coin that can be used to pay Binance fees, was down 5% over the past 24 hours at $709.70, according to market aggregator CoinGecko. Shares in crypto exchange Coinbase Global slid 4.8% while those of bitcoin buyer Strategy fell nearly 6% in extended US trading. The incident could be the world's biggest crypto heist, according to analytics firm Chainalysis and other industry experts. "It's the biggest hack in history," said Aravind Srinivasan, head of large crypto market maker GSR's systematic ‌OTC business. Beyond the potential loss of assets, the security breach was ⁠likely to have wider ramifications for crypto, which had already been under pressure lately due to higher US interest rates and softer demand from exchange-traded fund buyers, analysts said. "It may further dampen risk appetite and prompt investors to reassess the safety of assets held on centralized exchanges, as well as counterparty, solvency ⁠and liquidity risks," said Tim Sun, senior researcher at HashKey Group, based in Hong Kong. Binance, which allows users to buy, sell and trade digital assets, has 335 million registered users globally and had about $162.8 billion in assets under custody as of the exchange's 2025 annual report. "User funds remain safe," Binance said in a statement. "As a precaution, all deposits and withdrawals are temporarily suspended while our security teams conduct checks, secure wallet infrastructure, and trace affected ​assets, ​with the close support of our law enforcement and industry partners." Binance runs a secure ​asset fund for users, which is a reserve held entirely in bitcoin that ‌is intended to protect user assets in cases of security breaches, according to its website. "It's becoming very hard to counter hacks as AI can find vulnerabilities faster than you can fix them," said Bernardo Brites, CEO of Trace Finance, a payments and stablecoin infrastructure company. "My view is that users will move away from smaller and medium-sized exchanges, (it is) becoming too risky to park your money somewhere that couldn't cover a hack of meaningful size." Stablecoin issuer Tether said it had frozen nearly $1.57 billion in assets linked to the incident, while Circle froze more than $800 million. World Liberty Financial, a crypto company linked to US President Donald Trump and his family, said on Thursday it had worked with cryptocurrency custodian BitGo to freeze funds stolen in what it described as a Binance hack. Binance's Yi said $27 million in stablecoins ‌and about $2 million worth of World Liberty tokens had been frozen. Crypto firm Ripple also froze roughly $200 million in ​funds, Yi said. Jack McDonald, senior vice president of stablecoins at Ripple, said the company was closely monitoring reports of ​a potential exploit involving Binance and was freezing affected funds and coordinating with relevant parties. Miguel Morel, CEO of blockchain intelligence firm Arkham, said data indicated that billions of dollars appeared to have been hacked from Binance ‌by an unknown actor. The incident adds to a string of crypto thefts. ​Last year, attackers stole $2.9 billion worth of cryptocurrency across ​nearly 150 attacks, according to researchers at TRM Labs. In September, cryptocurrency exchange Bitget said roughly $350 million in crypto had been stolen from its platform, underscoring the industry's vulnerability to hackers. Authorities have warned that organised crime groups are increasingly using cryptocurrencies to move funds across borders outside the traditional financial system. Binance.US, a separate cryptocurrency exchange, said it was not affected by ​the security incident. Coinbase said it was unaffected and was monitoring the situation. In ‌an unrelated incident earlier on Thursday, prediction market operator Polymarket temporarily halted trading after a security incident involving a third-party provider. It later resumed trading and said it ​would fully reimburse affected traders. (Reporting by Tom Westbrook, Ankur Banerjee Raw Wee in Singapore, Summer Zhen in Hong Kong, Vallari Srivastava and Anusha Shah in Bengaluru and Mrinmay ​Dey in Mexico City; Writing by Scott Murdoch; Editing by Michelle Price, Sherry Jacob-Phillips and Jamie Freed)

Binance.US, a separate cryptocurrency exchange, said it was not affected by ​the security incident.

extraction.body: The world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, Binance, has frozen around $3 billion worth of digital assets after reporting a potential security breach. The incident has also prompted two major cryptocurrency firms, Tether and Circle, to freeze another $2.4 billion in assets linked to the suspected attack. Binance has temporarily suspended all deposits and withdrawals as its security teams investigate the incident. The company has also assured users that it will cover all losses arising from the security issue. The scale of the potential breach remains unclear. Blockchain analytics firms have estimated that the incident could involve more than $5 billion in stolen cryptocurrency, although Binance has not confirmed how much, if any, has been stolen. The security incident concerns Binance.com, the company's main global trading platform. Its US-focused subsidiary, Binance.US, said it was not affected. The developments have unsettled cryptocurrency markets. Bitcoin fell to a six-week low of $77,646 on Friday, October 30, while Ether dropped to a two-month low of $2,238.76, according to CoinGecko data cited by Reuters. Binance's native token, BNB, also fell more than 8 per cent over 24 hours to around $694. Binance said its teams had frozen approximately $3 billion worth of digital assets as part of efforts to contain the security incident. The exchange is working with law enforcement agencies, cryptocurrency issuers, blockchain intelligence firms and other industry partners to trace and freeze additional assets. The amount could increase as the investigation progresses. Two major cryptocurrency companies have also taken action. Tether, the issuer of the USDT stablecoin, said it had frozen around $1.6 billion in assets connected to the potential Binance hack. Circle, which issues the USDC stablecoin, said it had frozen more than $800 million linked to the incident. Together, the two companies have frozen around $2.4 billion in assets. The potential scale of the incident remains a major concern for the cryptocurrency industry. Glassnode, a digital asset analytics and advisory firm, estimated that the incident could involve around $5.3 billion in cryptocurrency. New York-based blockchain analytics firm Chainalysis put the estimated amount at more than $5.9 billion. These figures have not been confirmed by Binance and should not be treated as verified losses. If the higher estimate is established, the incident would rank among the largest cryptocurrency thefts on record. That incident resulted in losses of around $1.5 billion and has been attributed to hackers linked to North Korea. Binance has not disclosed the precise nature of the vulnerability or explained how the suspected attackers may have gained access to the assets. The company's former chief executive Changpeng Zhao also weighed in on the incident. "It does look like a hack," Zhao said in a post on X. He no longer runs Binance but remains a major shareholder in the company. What has Binance said about the security breach? Binance initially said its teams were investigating reports of a potential security issue and assured customers that their funds were safe. The company subsequently announced that it had frozen around $3 billion in assets. As a precaution, it suspended deposits and withdrawals while its security teams conducted checks and worked with law enforcement agencies to trace the funds. Binance also promised to compensate users for any losses. Binance will cover all losses," the company said in an update on X. It added that it was working around the clock and would publish a detailed post-mortem report once the investigation was complete. Why have Bitcoin and other cryptocurrencies fallen?

extraction.body: The world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, Binance, has frozen around $3 billion worth of digital assets after reporting a potential security breach. The incident has also prompted two major cryptocurrency firms, Tether and Circle, to freeze another $2.4 billion in assets linked to the suspected attack. Binance has temporarily suspended all deposits and withdrawals as its security teams investigate the incident. The company has also assured users that it will cover all losses arising from the security issue. The scale of the potential breach remains unclear. Blockchain analytics firms have estimated that the incident could involve more than $5 billion in stolen cryptocurrency, although Binance has not confirmed how much, if any, has been stolen. The security incident concerns Binance.com, the company's main global trading platform. Its US-focused subsidiary, Binance.US, said it was not affected. The developments have unsettled cryptocurrency markets. Bitcoin fell to a six-week low of $77,646 on Friday, October 30, while Ether dropped to a two-month low of $2,238.76, according to CoinGecko data cited by Reuters. Binance's native token, BNB, also fell more than 8 per cent over 24 hours to around $694. Binance said its teams had frozen approximately $3 billion worth of digital assets as part of efforts to contain the security incident. The exchange is working with law enforcement agencies, cryptocurrency issuers, blockchain intelligence firms and other industry partners to trace and freeze additional assets. The amount could increase as the investigation progresses. Two major cryptocurrency companies have also taken action. Tether, the issuer of the USDT stablecoin, said it had frozen around $1.6 billion in assets connected to the potential Binance hack. Circle, which issues the USDC stablecoin, said it had frozen more than $800 million linked to the incident. Together, the two companies have frozen around $2.4 billion in assets. The potential scale of the incident remains a major concern for the cryptocurrency industry. Glassnode, a digital asset analytics and advisory firm, estimated that the incident could involve around $5.3 billion in cryptocurrency. New York-based blockchain analytics firm Chainalysis put the estimated amount at more than $5.9 billion. These figures have not been confirmed by Binance and should not be treated as verified losses. If the higher estimate is established, the incident would rank among the largest cryptocurrency thefts on record. That incident resulted in losses of around $1.5 billion and has been attributed to hackers linked to North Korea. Binance has not disclosed the precise nature of the vulnerability or explained how the suspected attackers may have gained access to the assets. The company's former chief executive Changpeng Zhao also weighed in on the incident. "It does look like a hack," Zhao said in a post on X. He no longer runs Binance but remains a major shareholder in the company. What has Binance said about the security breach? Binance initially said its teams were investigating reports of a potential security issue and assured customers that their funds were safe. The company subsequently announced that it had frozen around $3 billion in assets. As a precaution, it suspended deposits and withdrawals while its security teams conducted checks and worked with law enforcement agencies to trace the funds. Binance also promised to compensate users for any losses. Binance will cover all losses," the company said in an update on X. It added that it was working around the clock and would publish a detailed post-mortem report once the investigation was complete. Why have Bitcoin and other cryptocurrencies fallen?

An initial investigation suggested the breach may have started with a hacked laptop belonging to one of its engineers, which let an attacker gain access to one of its systems and make unauthorized withdrawals, Binance said. Markets reacted immediately in early ​Asian trading on Friday. Bitcoin dropped more than 3% to a six-week low of $76,368 and ether fell more than 3% to a two-month low of $2,178. BNB, a token originally launched as Binance Coin that can be used to pay Binance fees, was down 5% over the past 24 hours at $709.70, according to market aggregator CoinGecko. Shares in crypto exchange Coinbase Global slid 4.8% while those of bitcoin buyer Strategy fell nearly 6% in extended US trading. The incident could be the world's biggest crypto heist, according to analytics firm Chainalysis and other industry experts. "It's the biggest hack in history," said Aravind Srinivasan, head of large crypto market maker GSR's systematic ‌OTC business. Beyond the potential loss of assets, the security breach was ⁠likely to have wider ramifications for crypto, which had already been under pressure lately due to higher US interest rates and softer demand from exchange-traded fund buyers, analysts said. "It may further dampen risk appetite and prompt investors to reassess the safety of assets held on centralized exchanges, as well as counterparty, solvency ⁠and liquidity risks," said Tim Sun, senior researcher at HashKey Group, based in Hong Kong. Binance, which allows users to buy, sell and trade digital assets, has 335 million registered users globally and had about $162.8 billion in assets under custody as of the exchange's 2025 annual report. "User funds remain safe," Binance said in a statement. "As a precaution, all deposits and withdrawals are temporarily suspended while our security teams conduct checks, secure wallet infrastructure, and trace affected ​assets, ​with the close support of our law enforcement and industry partners." Binance runs a secure ​asset fund for users, which is a reserve held entirely in bitcoin that ‌is intended to protect user assets in cases of security breaches, according to its website. "It's becoming very hard to counter hacks as AI can find vulnerabilities faster than you can fix them," said Bernardo Brites, CEO of Trace Finance, a payments and stablecoin infrastructure company. "My view is that users will move away from smaller and medium-sized exchanges, (it is) becoming too risky to park your money somewhere that couldn't cover a hack of meaningful size." Stablecoin issuer Tether said it had frozen nearly $1.57 billion in assets linked to the incident, while Circle froze more than $800 million. World Liberty Financial, a crypto company linked to US President Donald Trump and his family, said on Thursday it had worked with cryptocurrency custodian BitGo to freeze funds stolen in what it described as a Binance hack. Binance's Yi said $27 million in stablecoins ‌and about $2 million worth of World Liberty tokens had been frozen. Crypto firm Ripple also froze roughly $200 million in ​funds, Yi said. extraction.body: The world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, Binance, has frozen around $3 billion worth of digital assets after reporting a potential security breach. The incident has also prompted two major cryptocurrency firms, Tether and Circle, to freeze another $2.4 billion in assets linked to the suspected attack. Binance has temporarily suspended all deposits and withdrawals as its security teams investigate the incident. The company has also assured users that it will cover all losses arising from the security issue. The scale of the potential breach remains unclear. Blockchain analytics firms have estimated that the incident could involve more than $5 billion in stolen cryptocurrency, although Binance has not confirmed how much, if any, has been stolen. The security incident concerns Binance.com, the company's main global trading platform. Its US-focused subsidiary, Binance.US, said it was not affected. The developments have unsettled cryptocurrency markets. Bitcoin fell to a six-week low of $77,646 on Friday, October 30, while Ether dropped to a two-month low of $2,238.76, according to CoinGecko data cited by Reuters. Binance's native token, BNB, also fell more than 8 per cent over 24 hours to around $694. Binance said its teams had frozen approximately $3 billion worth of digital assets as part of efforts to contain the security incident. The exchange is working with law enforcement agencies, cryptocurrency issuers, blockchain intelligence firms and other industry partners to trace and freeze additional assets. The amount could increase as the investigation progresses. Two major cryptocurrency companies have also taken action. Tether, the issuer of the USDT stablecoin, said it had frozen around $1.6 billion in assets connected to the potential Binance hack. Circle, which issues the USDC stablecoin, said it had frozen more than $800 million linked to the incident. Together, the two companies have frozen around $2.4 billion in assets. The potential scale of the incident remains a major concern for the cryptocurrency industry. Glassnode, a digital asset analytics and advisory firm, estimated that the incident could involve around $5.3 billion in cryptocurrency. New York-based blockchain analytics firm Chainalysis put the estimated amount at more than $5.9 billion. These figures have not been confirmed by Binance and should not be treated as verified losses. If the higher estimate is established, the incident would rank among the largest cryptocurrency thefts on record. That incident resulted in losses of around $1.5 billion and has been attributed to hackers linked to North Korea. Binance has not disclosed the precise nature of the vulnerability or explained how the suspected attackers may have gained access to the assets. The company's former chief executive Changpeng Zhao also weighed in on the incident. "It does look like a hack," Zhao said in a post on X. He no longer runs Binance but remains a major shareholder in the company. What has Binance said about the security breach? Binance initially said its teams were investigating reports of a potential security issue and assured customers that their funds were safe. The company subsequently announced that it had frozen around $3 billion in assets. As a precaution, it suspended deposits and withdrawals while its security teams conducted checks and worked with law enforcement agencies to trace the funds. Binance also promised to compensate users for any losses. Binance will cover all losses," the company said in an update on X. It added that it was working around the clock and would publish a detailed post-mortem report once the investigation was complete. Why have Bitcoin and other cryptocurrencies fallen?

extraction.body: Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, said on Thursday that $2.54 billion worth of crypto assets had been frozen as it investigated a possible security breach. Stablecoin issuers Circle and Tether also froze assets linked to the incident, news agency Reuters reported."Binance will cover all hacking losses," Binance co-founder Yi He said.The exchange said the amount frozen could increase as it worked with law enforcement agencies, token issuers, blockchain intelligence firms and other industry partners to trace and freeze more assets.Binance co-founder Changpeng Zhao, who no longer runs the company, said in a post on X that the incident "looked like a hack."Tether said it had frozen nearly $1.57 billion in assets linked to the incident, while Circle froze more than $800 million.Binance said it was carrying out security checks and would resume withdrawals once the issue was fully resolved. It also assured users that their funds remained safe and said its teams were reviewing the incident. The exchange temporarily suspended trading on its Binance Alpha platform as a precaution.World Liberty Financial, a cryptocurrency company linked to US President Donald Trump and his family, said it had worked with crypto custodian BitGo to freeze funds stolen in what it described as a Binance hack.Yi He said $27 million in stablecoins and around $2 million worth of World Liberty tokens had been frozen.Crypto firm Ripple also froze around $200 million in funds, Yi said. Jack McDonald, senior vice president of stablecoins at Ripple, said the company was closely monitoring reports of a possible security breach involving Binance. He added that Ripple was freezing affected funds and coordinating with relevant parties.Miguel Morel, CEO of blockchain intelligence firm Arkham, said data suggested that billions of dollars may have been stolen from Binance by an unknown attacker. However, the exact cause of the incident had not been confirmed.Morel said the incident began around 4:30 pm EST and appeared to be ongoing.The incident adds to a series of cryptocurrency thefts. Attackers stole $2.9 billion worth of cryptocurrency in nearly 150 attacks last year, according to researchers at TRM Labs.In September, cryptocurrency exchange Bitget said around $350 million worth of crypto had been stolen from its platform, highlighting the security risks facing the industry.Authorities have warned that organised crime groups are increasingly using cryptocurrencies to move money across borders outside the traditional financial system.Binance allows users to buy, sell and trade digital assets. It has more than 300 million registered users globally and around $160 billion in assets under custody, according to the exchange's 2024 annual report.Binance.US, a separate cryptocurrency exchange, said it was not affected by the security incident. Coinbase also said it was unaffected and was monitoring the situation.In a separate incident on Thursday, prediction market operator Polymarket temporarily halted trading following a security issue involving a third-party provider. Trading later resumed, and the company said it would fully reimburse affected traders.You use AI every day.

extraction.body: French AI company Mistral has released the weights for its trillion-parameter open source AI model Mistral Large 4 (ML4), allowing businesses and governments to download and deploy the system themselves. Nicknamed “Le Chonk,” the model was first introduced earlier this month . The release comes as competition between open-weight AI developers like Mistral and closed-model providers like OpenAI and Anthropic heats up, with the former arguing that businesses and governments shouldn’t have to rely on outside AI companies for access to advanced capabilities. That argument may hold more weight in cybersecurity, where organizations want more control over their data and systems. Or, as Mistral’s CEO, Arthur Mensch, explained, AI should “be a tool for empowerment, not dominance.” With Chonk, Mistral doubles down on that position, arguing that it’s able to achieve “state-of-the-art performance” at a “fraction of the compute and capital committed by closed labs.” The release of the model’s weights — the numerical training that animates the system — ensures that other companies and government agencies will now be able to deploy ML4 for their own purposes. Mistral says that its model is comparable in terms of performance with a Chinese open-weight competitor, GLM-5.3, which was previously considered one of the best open-weight models in the world — particularly when it comes to cyber work. However, Mistral’s model uses 47 percent fewer tokens per task, making it significantly more economical than GLM-5.3. The company also claims that the model outranks all other open models when it comes to agentic coding tasks on Artificial Analysis’ Coding Agent Index, an AI benchmarking site. “Amid growing cyber threats, ML4 brings state-of-the-art sovereign cyber defense capabilities to enterprises and governments globally,” the company said Thursday. “Enterprise and public sector institutions can now download, deploy, and own frontier AI to detect, analyze, and respond to threats across code and IT infrastructure.” The weights for ML4 are being made available on Hugging Face and via its API. Pierre Stock, Vice President of Science at Mistral, told TechCrunch that the release of the model’s weights meant that organizations will have more control over how they use AI to defend themselves. “Concretely, it means that, for instance, as a business company or as a government, you’re able to have access to frontier intelligence to defend yourselves against cyberattacks. Access that can’t be cut off by definition because the model is open-weighted,” he said. Stock added that the model could be used to “identify, coordinate, and respond in real time to major security incidents, and that the open sourcing means that companies can deploy this model on-prem in their own ecosystem. While advances in AI cybersecurity are helping security professionals to find bugs at a much higher rate than before, Stock continued, he believes it’s important for companies to “provide [this same] capability to everyone…as soon as possible to ramp up and to strengthen the ecosystem,” given that “some malicious actors might try to actually leverage their own technology to attack.” Separately, Stock addressed concerns about recent incidents involving rogue AI agents, acknowledging the risks but cautioning against overreacting. “We don’t want to fearmonger people. We think it’s a problem that is solvable. It’s a hard problem to have good security,” he said. The company published the open-weight model as a 1 trillion-parameter, natively multimodal system, and its pitch leans hard on cyber defense instead of general chat.
Mistral reported that Large 4 scores 51% on the Artificial Analysis Cyber Index, a third-party benchmark.
Independent indices carry more weight than a lab’s internal tests, so this figure deserves attention.
A raw percentage still tells you little without the comparison set, and the fact sheet we hold does not include scores for rival models on the same index.
Open-weight releases have become the main battleground between labs that sell hosted access and labs that hand customers the files.
This analysis walks through what Mistral confirmed, what the numbers do and do not prove, and who gains or loses from putting a cyber-capable model in everyone’s hands.
A staged rollout like that gives a lab time to gather feedback, harden safeguards and brief partners before the files become permanent public property.
It also lets competitors read the preview and prepare responses.
Mistral built its reputation in Europe by shipping open models while US rivals kept their best systems behind APIs.
Large 4 pushes that approach to the trillion-parameter scale and adds an explicit cyber focus.
Open-weight AI has moved from a hobbyist niche to a core piece of national and corporate strategy within a few years.
Open weights build trust and adoption, while the API and enterprise support line up the revenue.
The company has not published financial details about Large 4, and we make no claims about them.
Several questions remain open at publication time.
Mistral’s cited materials give no API price.
We also found no independent reproduction of the 82% vulnerability result or the 96.6% refusal figure.
Those two sentences capture the whole debate.
Stock defends openness as a principle, and he concedes that a downloaded file cannot be recalled.
Mistral calls the model “Le Chonk” in its own announcement.
It first previewed the system on October 6, so the gap between preview and public weights came to 23 days.
Mistral described Large 4 as “one of the world’s strongest AI models for cybersecurity.” It also says the model tells defensive security tasks apart from malicious, offensive ones.
That second claim carries most of the weight in the sales pitch, because a model that helps a defender patch a bug can, in principle, help an attacker write an exploit for the same bug.
We hold no verified head-to-head scores, so we will not invent a leaderboard.
Benchmarks will decide how fast that pressure builds.
If independent labs confirm the 51% and 82% figures, procurement teams will start adding Large 4 to shortlists.
If the numbers shrink under neutral testing, the launch will read as a strong marketing move on top of a decent model.
A common pattern is a hosted frontier model for general work and a self-hosted open model for anything that touches secrets, source code or incident data.
That split shapes who actually benefits from the open weights in the first year.
The honest framing is that open weights trade vendor-side guardrails for customer-side control, and each buyer must decide which risk they fear more.
You can see that framing in the ZDNET report on the weights release .
The confirmed hardware-agnostic specs are short but significant.
That design lets a lab claim a trillion parameters without paying the compute bill of a dense trillion-parameter model on every request.
It also handles text and other inputs natively, rather than bolting a vision module onto a language model afterward.
If large customers self-host, hyperscalers still win GPU rental revenue, but they lose the model margin that sits on top.
Expect cloud platforms to list Large 4 in their model catalogs quickly, since refusing to would push customers elsewhere.
Readers should treat the number as a snapshot.
Benchmarks in this area move quickly, since labs tune for them and new tasks get added.
A 51% score means the model passes about half of what the index asks, and the index itself defines what counts as success.
Anyone buying on the strength of one score should ask for the task list and run a pilot on their own code.
Cybersecurity makes the move sharper than a general model release.

extraction.body: Mistral AI put the weights of Mistral Large 4 online on October 29, 2026, and the French lab aimed the release squarely at security teams. The company published the open-weight model as a 1 trillion-parameter, natively multimodal system, and its pitch leans hard on cyber defense instead of general chat. Reuters reported the release under the headline Mistral AI publicly releases Large 4, targets cybersecurity users . Mistral calls the model “Le Chonk” in its own announcement. It first previewed the system on October 6, so the gap between preview and public weights came to 23 days. That timing matters. Open-weight releases have become the main battleground between labs that sell hosted access and labs that hand customers the files. Our open-weight model license comparison covered six families before this launch, and Large 4 now adds a new heavyweight to that list. This analysis walks through what Mistral confirmed, what the numbers do and do not prove, and who gains or loses from putting a cyber-capable model in everyone’s hands. The release has two parts. Mistral posted the model weights for download on Hugging Face, and it also serves the same model through its own API. Developers who want to run the system on their own hardware can pull the files. Teams that prefer a hosted endpoint can call it the usual way. Mistral framed the move in plain terms in its announcement: “We release the weights of Le Chonk, advancing the frontier of open models in agentic coding and cybersecurity.” The sentence names two target workloads, and neither is casual conversation. Agentic coding means a model that writes, runs and fixes code across many steps. Cybersecurity means finding, reproducing and patching software flaws. Mistral also described the model as the best open agentic coding model in the world, according to its official materials. It said enterprises and governments get “frontier AI cyber defence capabilities they can fully own and control.” Those are company claims, and independent reviewers will need weeks to test them. Still, the framing tells you who Mistral wants as customers: security operations teams, public agencies and regulated firms that cannot send sensitive code to a third-party cloud. One detail remains unconfirmed. Mistral’s cited release materials do not state a price for API access, so any per-token figure circulating today lacks a source. We will update this report if Mistral publishes rates. The confirmed hardware-agnostic specs are short but significant. Large 4 uses a Mixture-of-Experts architecture, which means only part of the network activates for each token. That design lets a lab claim a trillion parameters without paying the compute bill of a dense trillion-parameter model on every request. It also handles text and other inputs natively, rather than bolting a vision module onto a language model afterward. A 1M context window changes what a security workflow can look like. A reviewer can feed an entire mid-sized codebase, its dependency manifest and a stack of recent advisories into one prompt. Whether the model keeps its accuracy at that length is a separate question that only independent testing will answer. Mistral has not published a long-context accuracy curve in the materials we reviewed. The size also sets a practical floor for self-hosting. A model with a trillion parameters needs serious multi-GPU infrastructure even when only a fraction of the experts fire per token. Small teams will most likely use the API, while governments, large banks and telecom carriers can justify the cluster. That split shapes who actually benefits from the open weights in the first year. Mistral described Large 4 as “one of the world’s strongest AI models for cybersecurity.” It also says the model tells defensive security tasks apart from malicious, offensive ones. That second claim carries most of the weight in the sales pitch, because a model that helps a defender patch a bug can, in principle, help an attacker write an exploit for the same bug. Mistral co-founder Guillaume Lample made the strategic case in launch coverage. He said the cyber defense capabilities will let enterprises and governments defend themselves against threat actors who are jailbreaking closed models to perform cyberattacks. The argument runs like this: attackers already have access to capable models through jailbreaks, so defenders deserve a model they can run, inspect and tune on their own terms. Based on Mistral’s official framing, three buyer groups stand out. Security operations centers want faster triage and patch drafting. Software vendors want automated bug reproduction before a release ships. Government agencies want a model that never leaves their network. Each group values control over raw leaderboard rank, which explains why Mistral led with ownership language instead of a speed claim. Mistral reported that Large 4 scores 51% on the Artificial Analysis Cyber Index, a third-party benchmark. Independent indices carry more weight than a lab’s internal tests, so this figure deserves attention. A raw percentage still tells you little without the comparison set, and the fact sheet we hold does not include scores for rival models on the same index. Readers should treat the number as a snapshot. Benchmarks in this area move quickly, since labs tune for them and new tasks get added. A 51% score means the model passes about half of what the index asks, and the index itself defines what counts as success. Anyone buying on the strength of one score should ask for the task list and run a pilot on their own code. The 3.4% line in the table is our own subtraction, not a Mistral claim. It assumes the refusal rate is a simple average across the test prompts. Even if that is true, a defender can live with a small leak, while a determined attacker only needs one useful answer. The second headline number is 82%. Mistral says Large 4 reached that score on a test where the model reproduces a real vulnerability in open-source software and then patches it. Reproduction is the hard part. A model has to read the bug report, build or locate a failing input and prove the flaw triggers, and only then write a fix that removes it without breaking the rest of the program. That end-to-end shape matters more than a multiple-choice security quiz. Real defenders spend most of their time on exactly this loop. They confirm that a reported flaw is real, they judge its reach and they ship a patch that maintainers will accept. A model that automates even part of it could cut the queue of open advisories that every security team complains about. Closed models face their own leak. Lample’s point about jailbreaks is real, and our report on DeepSeek and Moonshot’s use of GPT-6 Astra showed how capabilities travel even when access is gated. Neither route gives perfect control. The honest framing is that open weights trade vendor-side guardrails for customer-side control, and each buyer must decide which risk they fear more. Mistral executives did not dodge the downside. Pierre Stock, Mistral’s Vice President of Science, told Reuters: “I’m not comfortable living in a world in which open weights do not exist.” He also acknowledged the flip side of a public release. Once the model is out, he said, “it’s impossible to contain access.” Those two sentences capture the whole debate. Stock defends openness as a principle, and he concedes that a downloaded file cannot be recalled. Fortune reported a related claim from him after the launch, that Large 4 is the best open-weight model on cyber and coding. Read together, the comments show a company that knows the trade and has decided to accept it, in a Fortune report on the launch that frames the model as a top open option for agentic coding and cyber defense. Governments are watching the same trade from the other side. Our piece on China’s open-weight AI as weapon or armour lays out how one major power treats open releases as strategy. A Western lab shipping a cyber-capable trillion-parameter model changes the terms of that argument, because the same capability now sits in both camps. The practical effect is a faster diffusion of skill. Before this week, a mid-tier attacker needed to rent hosted access or jailbreak it. Now the attacker can download a strong model, though running one at this size still takes real hardware and money. That cost barrier filters out hobbyists but not funded groups, and defenders should plan accordingly. Many large buyers will end up with both. A common pattern is a hosted frontier model for general work and a self-hosted open model for anything that touches secrets, source code or incident data. Large 4 gives that second slot a credible occupant for the first time at this capability tier. ZDNET’s headline on the launch says Mistral’s Le Chonk is now a top open model for coding, ranking alongside Codex GPT-6.1 Terra. You can see that framing in the ZDNET report on the weights release . The comparison puts an open model in the same sentence as a leading closed coding product, which would have sounded optimistic a year ago. We hold no verified head-to-head scores, so we will not invent a leaderboard. What we can say is that the open-weight field now has several serious entrants. Our earlier DeepSeek vs Qwen vs Mistral comparison mapped the options before Large 4 landed, and the new release raises the bar for all three families. The competitive pressure runs in two directions. Open-weight rivals must now answer on cyber tasks specifically, an area many of them skipped in their launch material. Closed vendors must justify their premium to buyers who can see a near-peer they can run themselves. Neither group can ignore a trillion-parameter model with a 1M window and a published cyber score. Benchmarks will decide how fast that pressure builds. If independent labs confirm the 51% and 82% figures, procurement teams will start adding Large 4 to shortlists. If the numbers shrink under neutral testing, the launch will read as a strong marketing move on top of a decent model. Mistral previewed Large 4 on October 6, 2026, and shipped the weights 23 days later. A staged rollout like that gives a lab time to gather feedback, harden safeguards and brief partners before the files become permanent public property. It also lets competitors read the preview and prepare responses. The release also fits a longer pattern. Mistral built its reputation in Europe by shipping open models while US rivals kept their best systems behind APIs. Large 4 pushes that approach to the trillion-parameter scale and adds an explicit cyber focus. Open-weight AI has moved from a hobbyist niche to a core piece of national and corporate strategy within a few years. Cybersecurity makes the move sharper than a general model release. A chatbot that writes a clumsy poem harms nobody. A model that can reproduce and patch a real vulnerability sits near the same tools that find and weaponize one. That dual-use shadow explains why the same week produced both enthusiastic coverage and pointed questions about containment. Cloud providers face a subtler effect. If large customers self-host, hyperscalers still win GPU rental revenue, but they lose the model margin that sits on top. Expect cloud platforms to list Large 4 in their model catalogs quickly, since refusing to would push customers elsewhere. We could not confirm any such listing at publication time, so treat that as an expectation and not a report. Mistral itself gets a different payoff. Open weights build trust and adoption, while the API and enterprise support line up the revenue. The company has not published financial details about Large 4, and we make no claims about them. Several questions remain open at publication time. Mistral’s cited materials give no API price. They do not list rival scores on the Cyber Index in the sources we reviewed. We also found no independent reproduction of the 82% vulnerability result or the 96.6% refusal figure. It is Mistral AI’s 1 trillion-parameter, natively multimodal Mixture-of-Experts model with a 1M context window. Mistral also calls it “Le Chonk.” The company released its weights publicly on October 29, 2026. Mistral previewed Large 4 on October 6, 2026. The public weights followed on October 29, 23 days later.
